definition: Widely repeated as true but of doubtful origin and probably made up.
example: The apocryphal story of the chef who invented the dish by accident is printed on every menu.
nuance: Unlike false, apocryphal describes a widely told story whose truth is doubtful or unproven, not one that has simply been shown to be wrong.
prompt: A tour guide tells visitors a famous story about the old lighthouse keeper.
options: Historians call the guide's tale of a midnight rescue apocryphal, as no record of it exists.
An apocryphal storm once destroyed the lighthouse and every cottage along the coast.
The guide called the keeper's signed logbook apocryphal because three archives had confirmed it.
The guide grew apocryphal when visitors asked questions, refusing to believe a word they said.
reasons: A popular story with no evidence behind it is exactly the kind of tale the word describes.
This confuses the word with apocalyptic; it says nothing about doubtful truth.
Confirmation by archives makes a source reliable, the reverse of what the word suggests.
The word describes stories that are doubted, not a person who doubts others.

practice.prompt: A class looks into a motto the town's founder supposedly carved above the school door.
options: The motto is apocryphal: the founder's own diary records him carving it in 1852.
The students felt apocryphal about the whole project and doubted every single source the librarian handed them.
The apocryphal motto predicted that the world would end in a great flood.
The students decided the motto was apocryphal, since it first appeared in print long after the founder died.
reasons: A firsthand diary entry is strong evidence, so the motto would be well documented, not doubtful.
This treats the word as a synonym for skeptical; it describes claims, not people's feelings.
This mixes the word up with apocalyptic, which concerns the end of the world.
A saying that shows up only long after the fact, with no early source, has a doubtful origin.
